change.excerpt: Gradivus knew that this was a signal given to him for the promised removal; and, leaning on his lance, he boldly mounted {behind} his steeds, laden with the blood-stained pole {of the chariot}, and urged them on with the lash of the whip; and descending along the steep air, he stood on the summit of the hill of the woody Palatium; and he took away the son of Ilia, that moment giving out his royal ordinances to his own Quirites. His mortal body glided through the yielding air; just as the leaden plummet, discharged from the broad sling, is wont to dissolve itself[62] in mid air. A beauteous appearance succeeded, one more suitable to the lofty couches[63] of heaven, and a form, such as that of Quirinus arrayed in his regal robe.

narrativeBlocks.title: Rome's own father
narrativeBlocks.body: Mars is no distant war-god to the Romans: he is the literal father of Romulus and Remus, the twins who founded the city — the divine bloodline starts at the top.

narrativeBlocks.title: The god collects his son
narrativeBlocks.body: At Mars's own request, Jupiter takes up Romulus in a whirlwind and fire — the mortal king is dissolved from mortal substance and made divine.

narrativeBlocks.title: From king to Quirinus
narrativeBlocks.body: Ovid describes the change precisely: the mortal parts burn away, and what remains is the god Quirinus — Rome's founder made Rome's own deity.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why a deified founder matters
narrativeBlocks.body: For Romans this was state theology, not just story: Quirinus means the city has divine ancestry and a divine protector in one figure — mythic legitimation for the empire itself.

narrativeBlocks.title: Rome writes its own myth
narrativeBlocks.body: Unlike Greece's remote heroes, Roman myth claims the gods are literally its founders and its emperors — and Ovid makes that political claim into verse.
